Almost every vector-geometry question is solved the same way: find a [[blue:ROUTE]] from the start point to the end point along vectors you already know, then simplify.

Parallel and collinear proofs then come down to spotting that one simplified vector is a multiple of another.

theory_blocks.title: Position vectors
theory_blocks.body:
Choose a fixed point $O$, the **origin**. The **position vector** of a point $A$ is $\overrightarrow{OA}$, usually written $\mathbf a$; likewise $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$.

For a point with coordinates $(x,y)$, the position vector is the column $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$.

To go from $A$ to $B$ you can go via the origin: back from $A$ to $O$, then out to $B$.
$$\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{AO}+\overrightarrow{OB}=-\mathbf a+\mathbf b=\mathbf b-\mathbf a.$$
In words: the vector from $A$ to $B$ is *position vector of the end minus position vector of the start*. In the figure, $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$.

assets.caption: $O$, $A(2,3)$ and $B(5,1)$: the position vectors $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$, and $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$.
assets.purpose: Make the 'via the origin' route for AB=b-a visible before the rule is used in calculations.

theory_blocks.title: Expressing vectors: routes and the triangle law
theory_blocks.body:
Whenever $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ are given, every other vector in the diagram can be written in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. Two facts do all the work:
- **Triangle law:** $\overrightarrow{XY}+\overrightarrow{YZ}=\overrightarrow{XZ}$.
- **Reversal:** $\overrightarrow{YX}=-\overrightarrow{XY}$. Travelling AGAINST an arrow gives a minus sign.

**Route method.** (1) Mark the two given vectors on the diagram with arrows. (2) To find $\overrightarrow{XY}$, choose a route from $X$ to $Y$ that uses only known vectors (often via $O$). (3) Add the vectors met along the route, with a minus sign for each one travelled backwards. (4) Simplify, collecting the multiples of $\mathbf a$ and of $\mathbf b$. If the route involves a fraction of a line, write that fraction times the whole vector first.

assets.caption: In triangle $OAB$, $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is found by the route $A\to O\to B$: $\overrightarrow{AB}=-\mathbf a+\mathbf b$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$.
assets.purpose: Show the triangle-law route for AB and preview the midpoint result used in the next section.

theory_blocks.title: Three errors to avoid with routes
theory_blocks.body:
- Writing $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$. It is [[blue:*end minus start*]]: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$.
- Forgetting the minus sign when a route goes against an arrow, for example $\overrightarrow{BO}=-\mathbf b$, not $\mathbf b$.
- Not simplifying: leave the answer as $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$ or $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$, not as a chain of unsimplified terms.

theory_blocks.title: Points that divide a line in a ratio
theory_blocks.body:
If a point $P$ lies on $AB$ with $AP:PB=m:n$, then $P$ is $\dfrac{m}{m+n}$ of the way from $A$ to $B$, so
$$\overrightarrow{AP}=\dfrac{m}{m+n}\overrightarrow{AB}.$$
The ratio $AP:PB=2:1$ means $AP=\tfrac23AB$, NOT $\tfrac12AB$ and NOT $2AB$. Always ADD the parts of the ratio to get the denominator: $2+1=3$.

Also check whether the ratio given is $AP:PB$ (part to part) or $AP:AB$ (part to whole) — they need a different fraction.

assets.caption: $P$ on $AB$ with $AP:PB=2:1$: the segment is split into $2+1=3$ equal parts, and $P$ is $\tfrac23$ of the way from $A$.
assets.purpose: Make the ratio-to-fraction conversion (adding the parts of the ratio) visible before it is used in a calculation.

theory_blocks.title: Parallel vectors and collinear points
theory_blocks.body:
**Parallel:** if $\overrightarrow{PQ}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$ for some scalar $k$, then $PQ$ and $AB$ are parallel, and $|PQ|=|k|\,|AB|$.

**Collinear:** three points $A$, $B$, $C$ are on one straight line if $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ are parallel, AND they share the point $B$. The proof therefore has two parts: (1) show $\overrightarrow{BC}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$; (2) say 'they are parallel and share the point $B$, so $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear'. Parallel alone is not enough: two separate, non-touching segments can easily be parallel without being part of the same line.

theory_blocks.title: Checking a route-method answer
theory_blocks.body:
After finding a vector, test it on a special case: take a simple triangle such as $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and see whether your answer gives the right coordinates.

For a midpoint result, $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1.5\end{pmatrix}$, which is indeed halfway between $(4,0)$ and $(0,3)$.

For the position vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ of a point $P$ on the line $AB$, the two coefficients of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ should always add to exactly $1$.

For a parallel or collinear test, factorise both vectors to show the same bracket, e.g. $3(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$ and $\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$: if you cannot write one vector as a number times the other, they are not parallel.

theory_blocks.title: Exam technique for staged vector-geometry questions
theory_blocks.body:
Exam questions often build in stages: 'Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$... Find $\overrightarrow{OM}$... Hence show that...'. Use the earlier parts in the later ones.

Write conclusions in WORDS ('$\overrightarrow{PQ}=\tfrac13\overrightarrow{AB}$, so $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$'); a correct algebra line without the concluding sentence can lose the final mark.

Give answers as simplified expressions in $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, written in bold (or underlined, or with an arrow) as in the paper.

theory_blocks.title: Operative summary
theory_blocks.body:
- $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$ (end minus start); $\overrightarrow{BA}=-\overrightarrow{AB}$; $\overrightarrow{XY}+\overrightarrow{YZ}=\overrightarrow{XZ}$.
- Midpoint of $AB$: $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$. If $AP:PB=m:n$, then $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac{m}{m+n}\overrightarrow{AB}$.
- Parallel: one vector is a scalar multiple of the other. Collinear: parallel AND share a point.
- If $\overrightarrow{PQ}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$, then $PQ=|k|\,AB$; a line parallel to a triangle's side cuts off a similar triangle (areas in ratio $k^2$).

keywords.definition: The vector $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ from a fixed origin $O$ to a point $A$.
$\overrightarrow{XY}+\overrightarrow{YZ}=\overrightarrow{XZ}$: the rule for combining two vectors travelled one after another.
A point $P$ on a line $AB$ dividing it in a given ratio $AP:PB=m:n$, with $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac{m}{m+n}\overrightarrow{AB}$.
Three or more points that all lie on a single straight line; proved by showing two vectors between them are parallel AND share a common point.
If $\overrightarrow{PQ}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$ with $P$, $Q$ on two sides of a triangle from $O$, triangles $OPQ$ and $OAB$ are similar with scale factor $k$ and area ratio $k^2:1$.

worked_examples.statement: Position vectors with coordinates. $A(2,3)$ and $B(5,1)$. Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and the position vector of the midpoint $M$ of $AB$.
reasoning: Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ as end minus start.
The midpoint is reached by going halfway along $\overrightarrow{AB}$ from $A$.
worked_examples.solution:
$\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$. The midpoint is halfway along $\overrightarrow{AB}$: $\overrightarrow{OM}=\mathbf a+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}1.5\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3.5\\2\end{pmatrix}$,

so $M=(3.5,\,2)$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check with the averages of the coordinates: $\tfrac{2+5}2=3.5$, $\tfrac{3+1}2=2$, which matches exactly.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Computing $\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ for $\overrightarrow{AB}$, which gives the vector from $B$ to $A$ instead.

worked_examples.statement:
Midpoint. In triangle $OAB$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Find, in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}$;

(b) $\overrightarrow{AM}$; (c) $\overrightarrow{OM}$.
reasoning: (a) Route $A\to O\to B$.
(b) $M$ is the midpoint, so $\overrightarrow{AM}$ is exactly half of $\overrightarrow{AB}$.
(c) Route $O\to A\to M$, using the answer to (b).
worked_examples.solution:
(a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{AO}+\overrightarrow{OB}=-\mathbf a+\mathbf b=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$.
(b) $\overrightarrow{AM}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}=\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$.
(c) $\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AM}=\mathbf a+\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac12\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf b=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result (c) says the position vector of a midpoint is the AVERAGE of the two position vectors — exactly the coordinate-midpoint formula, now proved using vectors.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Leaving the answer to (c) as $\mathbf a+\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$ without simplifying, instead of collecting it into $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$.

worked_examples.statement: Ratio. $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, and $P$ lies on $AB$ with $AP:PB=2:1$. Find $\overrightarrow{OP}$.
reasoning: Convert the ratio to a fraction of the whole line: $AP$ is $\tfrac{2}{2+1}=\tfrac23$ of $AB$.
Route $O\to A\to P$.
worked_examples.solution: $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac23(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$. Then $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AP}=\mathbf a+\tfrac23(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac13\mathbf a+\tfrac23\mathbf b$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: the coefficients $\tfrac13+\tfrac23=1$, as they must be for a point on the line $AB$; and $P$ is closer to $B$, so $\mathbf b$ has the larger coefficient.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using $AP:PB=2:1$ as the fraction $\tfrac21$ directly, instead of $\tfrac{2}{2+1}=\tfrac23$.

worked_examples.statement:
Show that lines are parallel; similarity. In triangle $OAB$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$. $P$ is on $OA$ with $OP:PA=1:2$ and $Q$ is on $OB$ with $OQ:QB=1:2$.

Show that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$ and find the ratio of their lengths.
reasoning: Convert each ratio: $OP:OA=1:3$ so $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac13\mathbf a$; similarly $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\tfrac13\mathbf b$.
Route $P\to O\to Q$ for $\overrightarrow{PQ}$, then compare with $\overrightarrow{AB}$.
worked_examples.solution:
$\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{PO}+\overrightarrow{OQ}=-\tfrac13\mathbf a+\tfrac13\mathbf b=\tfrac13(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac13\overrightarrow{AB}$.

So $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$: $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$, and $PQ=\tfrac13AB$ in length, so $PQ:AB=1:3$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Triangles $OPQ$ and $OAB$ are similar with scale factor $\tfrac13$; their areas are therefore in the ratio $1^2:3^2=1:9$. Note that $P,Q,A,B$ are NOT collinear here — $PQ$ and $AB$ are two different, parallel, non-touching segments.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding that $P$, $Q$, $A$, $B$ all lie on one line just because $PQ\parallel AB$, when in fact $PQ$ and $AB$ are two separate sides of similar triangles that never touch.

worked_examples.statement: Show that three points are collinear. $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\tfrac52\mathbf b-\tfrac32\mathbf a$. Show that $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on a straight line and find $AB:BC$.
reasoning: Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ separately (both share the point $B$).
Compare: is one a scalar multiple of the other?
worked_examples.solution:
$\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. $\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{BO}+\overrightarrow{OC}=-\mathbf b+\tfrac52\mathbf b-\tfrac32\mathbf a=\tfrac32\mathbf b-\tfrac32\mathbf a=\tfrac32(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$.

So $\overrightarrow{BC}=\tfrac32\overrightarrow{AB}$: the vectors are parallel, and they share the point $B$. Hence $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear.
worked_examples.interpretation: Since $BC=\tfrac32AB$, $AB:BC=1:\tfrac32=2:3$. Both conditions were checked: parallel (scalar multiple) AND a shared point ($B$) — stating both is required for full marks.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stopping at '$\overrightarrow{BC}=\tfrac32\overrightarrow{AB}$, so they are parallel' without the closing sentence naming the shared point and concluding collinearity explicitly, which can lose the final accuracy mark even with correct algebra.

guided_exercises.statement: $A(6,2)$ and $B(2,8)$ have position vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and the position vector of the midpoint $M$ of $AB$.
hints: Use end minus start: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$.
The midpoint's position vector is the AVERAGE of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2-6\\8-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\6\end{pmatrix}$. Midpoint: $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}8\\10\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\end{pmatrix}$, so $M=(4,5)$. Check with coordinate averages: $\tfrac{6+2}2=4$, $\tfrac{2+8}2=5$.
common_errors: Computing $\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ instead of $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$ for $\overrightarrow{AB}$.

guided_exercises.statement: In triangle $OAB$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$. $N$ is the point on $OB$ with $ON:NB=1:2$. Find, in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, (a) $\overrightarrow{ON}$; (b) $\overrightarrow{AN}$.
hints: $ON:NB=1:2$ means $ON$ is $\tfrac{1}{1+2}=\tfrac13$ of the whole of $OB$.
For $\overrightarrow{AN}$, use the route $A\to O\to N$.
common_errors: Using $ON=\tfrac12\mathbf b$ as if $N$ were the midpoint of $OB$, instead of converting the ratio $1:2$ to the fraction $\tfrac13$ of the whole line.

guided_exercises.statement: $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=3\mathbf a-2\mathbf b$. Show that $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear and find $AB:BC$.
hints: Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ (both involve the shared point $B$).
Check whether $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ — the scalar can be negative.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. $\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{BO}+\overrightarrow{OC}=-\mathbf b+3\mathbf a-2\mathbf b=3\mathbf a-3\mathbf b=-3(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=-3\overrightarrow{AB}$. So $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ (parallel, pointing the opposite way), and they share the point $B$; hence $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear, with $AB:BC=1:3$.
common_errors: Concluding the points are NOT collinear because the scalar $-3$ is negative, forgetting that a negative scalar still means parallel (just pointing the opposite way), which is still enough for collinearity once the shared point is checked.

exercises.statement: $A(3,2)$ and $B(-1,5)$ have position vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$ and the position vector of the midpoint of $AB$.
exercises.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\5\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\3\end{pmatrix}$; $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\sqrt{16+9}=5$; midpoint $=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3.5\end{pmatrix}$.
common_errors: Computing $\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ for $\overrightarrow{AB}$.

exercises.statement: $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, $M$ is the midpoint of $OB$. Write in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}$; (b) $\overrightarrow{BA}$; (c) $\overrightarrow{OM}$; (d) $\overrightarrow{AM}$.
exercises.answer: (a) $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$ (b) $\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ (c) $\tfrac12\mathbf b$ (d) $-\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf b$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. (b) $\overrightarrow{BA}=-\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$. (c) $M$ is the midpoint of $OB$, so $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12\mathbf b$. (d) $\overrightarrow{AM}=\overrightarrow{AO}+\overrightarrow{OM}=-\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf b$.
common_errors: In (c), confusing the midpoint of $OB$ with the midpoint of $AB$, and writing $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$ instead of $\tfrac12\mathbf b$.

exercises.statement: $OABC$ is a parallelogram with $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$. Find (a) $\overrightarrow{OB}$; (b) $\overrightarrow{AC}$; (c) $\overrightarrow{CB}$; (d) $\overrightarrow{OM}$ where $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$; (e) the position vector of the midpoint of the diagonal $AC$.
exercises.answer: (a) $\mathbf a+\mathbf c$ (b) $\mathbf c-\mathbf a$ (c) $\mathbf a$ (d) $\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf c$ (e) $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) In parallelogram $OABC$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf a+\mathbf c$. (b) $\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf c-\mathbf a$. (c) Opposite sides of the parallelogram are equal vectors, so $\overrightarrow{CB}=\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$. (d) $\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf c$ (since $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$ in a parallelogram). (e) Midpoint of $AC=\mathbf a+\tfrac12(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$ — the SAME point as the midpoint of the other diagonal $OB$, $\tfrac12\overrightarrow{OB}=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$, confirming the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
common_errors: In (c), finding $\overrightarrow{CB}$ by a full route calculation instead of noticing directly that opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal and parallel vectors.

exercises.statement: $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$. $P$ lies on $AB$ with $AP:PB=3:1$, and $Q$ lies on $AB$ with $AQ:QB=1:4$. Find $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$.
exercises.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf a+\tfrac34(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac14\mathbf a+\tfrac34\mathbf b$. $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\mathbf a+\tfrac15(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac45\mathbf a+\tfrac15\mathbf b$.
common_errors: Using $\tfrac34$ directly as the fraction for $Q$ too, instead of recomputing $\tfrac{1}{1+4}=\tfrac15$ for the different ratio $1:4$.

exercises.statement: Which of these vectors are parallel to each other? $6\mathbf a-3\mathbf b$, $2\mathbf a-\mathbf b$, $4\mathbf a+2\mathbf b$.
exercises.answer: $6\mathbf a-3\mathbf b$ and $2\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ are parallel to each other; $4\mathbf a+2\mathbf b$ is not parallel to either.
exercises.full_solution: $6\mathbf a-3\mathbf b=3(2\mathbf a-\mathbf b)$, so the first two are scalar multiples of each other: parallel. $4\mathbf a+2\mathbf b=2(2\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$, which is not a scalar multiple of $2\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ (the signs of the $\mathbf b$-term do not match), so it is not parallel to them.
common_errors: Declaring all three parallel simply because each is 'some combination of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$', without checking that one is actually a scalar multiple of another.

exercises.statement: $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, $\overrightarrow{OC}=4\mathbf b-3\mathbf a$. Show that $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear and find $AB:BC$.
exercises.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. $\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{BO}+\overrightarrow{OC}=-\mathbf b+4\mathbf b-3\mathbf a=3\mathbf b-3\mathbf a=3\overrightarrow{AB}$. Parallel and share $B$, so collinear; $AB:BC=1:3$.
common_errors: Stating only '$\overrightarrow{BC}=3\overrightarrow{AB}$, so they are parallel' without the closing sentence naming the shared point $B$ and the word 'collinear'.

exercises.statement: In triangle $OAB$, $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $OA$ and $OB$. Show that $MN$ is parallel to $AB$ and half its length.
exercises.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{ON}=\tfrac12\mathbf b$. $\overrightarrow{MN}=\overrightarrow{MO}+\overrightarrow{ON}=-\tfrac12\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf b=\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}$: a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, so parallel, with length exactly half.
common_errors: Treating this as a collinearity proof (it is not): $M$, $N$ lie on $OA$, $OB$ respectively and $MN$ is a SEPARATE, non-touching segment, parallel to but not part of the same line as $AB$.

exercises.statement: $OABC$ is a trapezium with $OA$ parallel to $CB$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$ and $CB=\tfrac12OA$ (same direction). Find (a) $\overrightarrow{OB}$; (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}$; (c) $\overrightarrow{OM}$, where $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$.
exercises.answer: (a) $\mathbf c+\tfrac12\mathbf a$ (b) $\mathbf c-\tfrac12\mathbf a$ (c) $\tfrac34\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf c$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\overrightarrow{CB}=\tfrac12\mathbf a$, so $\overrightarrow{OB}=\overrightarrow{OC}+\overrightarrow{CB}=\mathbf c+\tfrac12\mathbf a$. (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf c+\tfrac12\mathbf a-\mathbf a=\mathbf c-\tfrac12\mathbf a$. (c) $\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a+\tfrac12\left(\mathbf c-\tfrac12\mathbf a\right)=\tfrac34\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf c$.
common_errors: In (a), writing $\overrightarrow{CB}=\mathbf a$ instead of $\tfrac12\mathbf a$, forgetting the 'half the length' condition given in the question.

exercises.statement: Show that $A(1,2)$, $B(3,6)$ and $C(6,12)$ are collinear, and find $AB:BC$.
exercises.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\6\end{pmatrix}=\tfrac32\overrightarrow{AB}$; parallel with common point $B$, so collinear; $AB:BC=2:3$.
common_errors: Comparing only the $x$-components (or only the $y$-components) of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ to check 'parallel', instead of confirming the SAME scalar works for both components.

exercises.statement: $A(-2,1)$ and $B(8,6)$. $P$ lies on $AB$ with $AP:PB=2:3$. Find the coordinates of $P$.
exercises.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}10\\5\end{pmatrix}$; $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac25\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}$; $P=(-2+4,\,1+2)=(2,3)$.
common_errors: Using $\tfrac23$ as the fraction of $AB$ (treating the ratio numbers directly as the fraction) instead of $\tfrac{2}{2+3}=\tfrac25$.

exam_questions.statement:
$A(2,-3)$ and $B(8,9)$ have position vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$.
(a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$. [1]
(b) Find the position vector of the midpoint $M$ of $AB$. [2]
(c) $P$ lies on $AB$ with $AP:PB=1:2$. Find the coordinates of $P$. [3]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}6\\12\end{pmatrix}$. (b) $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)=\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\end{pmatrix}$, so $M=(5,3)$. (c) $AP:PB=1:2$, so $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac13\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\end{pmatrix}$; $P=(2+2,\,-3+4)=(4,1)$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $\begin{pmatrix}6\\12\end{pmatrix}$
(b) M1 for averaging the coordinates (or $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$); A1 for $(5,3)$
(c) M1 for converting the ratio $1:2$ to the fraction $\tfrac13$; M1 for adding $\tfrac13\overrightarrow{AB}$ to $A$'s coordinates; A1 for $(4,1)$
common_errors: In (c), using the fraction $\tfrac12$ (from the ratio $1:2$ read directly) instead of $\tfrac{1}{1+2}=\tfrac13$.

exam_questions.statement:
In triangle $OAB$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$. $M$ is on $OA$ with $OM:MA=1:3$, and $N$ is on $OB$ with $ON:NB=1:3$.
(a) Find $\overrightarrow{OM}$ and $\overrightarrow{ON}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. [2]
(b) Show that $MN$ is parallel to $AB$ and find the ratio $MN:AB$. [3]
(c) State the ratio of the area of triangle $OMN$ to the area of triangle $OAB$. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $OM:MA=1:3$ means $OM:OA=1:4$, so $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac14\mathbf a$; similarly $\overrightarrow{ON}=\tfrac14\mathbf b$. (b) $\overrightarrow{MN}=\overrightarrow{MO}+\overrightarrow{ON}=-\tfrac14\mathbf a+\tfrac14\mathbf b=\tfrac14(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac14\overrightarrow{AB}$: a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, so parallel, with $MN:AB=1:4$. (c) Triangles $OMN$ and $OAB$ are similar with scale factor $\tfrac14$, so their areas are in the ratio $\left(\tfrac14\right)^2:1^2=1:16$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for converting $OM:MA=1:3$ to $OM:OA=1:4$ correctly for both $M$ and $N$; A1 for both $\tfrac14\mathbf a$ and $\tfrac14\mathbf b$
(b) M1 for a correct route for $\overrightarrow{MN}$; A1 for the simplified $\tfrac14(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$; A1 for stating the ratio $1:4$ WITH the word 'parallel'
(c) B1 for using (scale factor)$^2$; B1 for $1:16$
common_errors: In (a), using the GIVEN ratio $1:3$ directly as the fraction of $OA$ (giving $\tfrac13\mathbf a$) instead of converting $OM:MA=1:3$ to $OM:OA=1:4$ first.

exam_questions.statement: $A(-1,-2)$, $B(5,4)$ and $C(k,10)$. Given that $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear, find the value of $k$, and find $AC:AB$.
exam_questions.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\6\end{pmatrix}$. $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}k+1\\12\end{pmatrix}$. For $A$, $B$, $C$ to be collinear, $\overrightarrow{AC}$ must be a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ (they share the point $A$): matching the $y$-components, $12=2\times6$, so the scalar is $2$; matching the $x$-components, $k+1=2\times6=12$, so $k=11$. Then $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}12\\12\end{pmatrix}=2\overrightarrow{AB}$, so $AC:AB=2:1$.
mark_scheme: M1 for finding $\overrightarrow{AB}$ correctly
M1 for setting up $\overrightarrow{AC}$ in terms of $k$
M1 for using the $y$-component to find the scalar multiplier ($2$)
A1 for $k=11$
A1 for the ratio $AC:AB=2:1$
common_errors: Finding the scalar multiplier from only one component (e.g. assuming it must be a 'nice' whole number) without checking it is consistent across BOTH components of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

exam_questions.statement:
The diagram shows the parallelogram $OABC$, in which $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, $N$ is the midpoint of $CB$, and $P$ is the midpoint of $MN$.
(a) Write $\overrightarrow{OB}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf c$. [1]
(b) Find $\overrightarrow{MN}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf c$, giving your answer in its simplest form. [2]
(c) Hence show that $MN$ is parallel to $AC$, and write down the ratio $MN:AC$. [2]
(d) Show that $O$, $P$ and $B$ lie on the same straight line, and find the ratio $OP:PB$. [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\mathbf a+\mathbf c$. (b) $\overrightarrow{MN}=\tfrac12(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)$. (c) $\overrightarrow{MN}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AC}$, a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AC}$, so $MN$ is parallel to $AC$; $MN:AC=1:2$. (d) $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac34(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)=\tfrac34\overrightarrow{OB}$, so $O$, $P$ and $B$ are collinear; $OP:PB=3:1$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $AB$ is parallel to $OC$ and the same length, so $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf c$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a+\mathbf c$.
(b) $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $\overrightarrow{OM}=\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf c$; $N$ is the midpoint of $CB$, so $\overrightarrow{ON}=\mathbf c+\tfrac12\mathbf a$. Then $\overrightarrow{MN}=\overrightarrow{ON}-\overrightarrow{OM}=\left(\tfrac12\mathbf a+\mathbf c\right)-\left(\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf c\right)=-\tfrac12\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf c=\tfrac12(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)$.
(c) $\overrightarrow{AC}=\overrightarrow{OC}-\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf c-\mathbf a$, so $\overrightarrow{MN}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AC}$. One vector is a scalar multiple of the other, so $MN$ is parallel to $AC$, and the lengths are in the ratio $MN:AC=1:2$.
(d) $P$ is the midpoint of $MN$, so $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac12\left(\overrightarrow{OM}+\overrightarrow{ON}\right)=\tfrac12\left(\tfrac32\mathbf a+\tfrac32\mathbf c\right)=\tfrac34(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)=\tfrac34\overrightarrow{OB}$. Since $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is a multiple of $\overrightarrow{OB}$ and both begin at $O$, the points $O$, $P$ and $B$ lie on one straight line. Also $\overrightarrow{PB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac14(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$, so $OP:PB=\tfrac34:\tfrac14=3:1$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $\mathbf a+\mathbf c$

(b) M1 for a correct route for $\overrightarrow{MN}$, e.g. $\overrightarrow{ON}-\overrightarrow{OM}$ or $\overrightarrow{MB}+\overrightarrow{BN}$, with correct expressions for the parts used; A1 for $\tfrac12(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)$ or $\tfrac12\mathbf c-\tfrac12\mathbf a$
(c) B1 for $\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf c-\mathbf a$ with the statement that $\overrightarrow{MN}$ is a scalar multiple of it, hence parallel; B1 for $MN:AC=1:2$

(d) M1 for $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac12\left(\overrightarrow{OM}+\overrightarrow{ON}\right)$ or $\overrightarrow{OM}+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{MN}$; A1 for $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac34(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$ identified as $\tfrac34\overrightarrow{OB}$, so $O$, $P$, $B$ are collinear; A1 for $OP:PB=3:1$
common_errors: In (c), writing only '$MN$ is parallel to $AC$' without showing that $\overrightarrow{MN}$ is a multiple of $\overrightarrow{AC}$; a 'show that' part is marked on the reason, not the conclusion.
In (d), stopping at $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac34(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$ and never comparing it with $\overrightarrow{OB}$, so the collinearity is asserted rather than shown.

assets.caption: Parallelogram $OABC$ with $M$ the midpoint of $AB$, $N$ the midpoint of $CB$ and $P$ the midpoint of $MN$; the diagonals $OB$ and $AC$ are dashed.
assets.purpose: Give the printed figure the question is read from, so the routes for $\overrightarrow{MN}$ and $\overrightarrow{OP}$ have to be taken off the diagram.

exam_questions.statement:
The diagram shows a regular hexagon $ABCDEF$ with centre $O$, where $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$. The long diagonal $AD$ passes through $O$, and $O$ is its midpoint. $M$ is the midpoint of $BD$.
(a) Write down, in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, (i) $\overrightarrow{AB}$, (ii) $\overrightarrow{OD}$. [2]
(b) Find $\overrightarrow{BD}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. [2]
(c) Find $\overrightarrow{OM}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. Hence show that $OM$ is parallel to $AB$, and write down the ratio $OM:AB$. [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a)(i) $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$; (ii) $-\mathbf a$. (b) $\overrightarrow{BD}=-\mathbf a-\mathbf b$. (c) $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}$, a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, so $OM$ is parallel to $AB$; $OM:AB=1:2$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a)(i) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{AO}+\overrightarrow{OB}=-\mathbf a+\mathbf b=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. (ii) $O$ is the midpoint of $AD$, so $\overrightarrow{OD}$ is the same length as $\overrightarrow{OA}$ but in the opposite direction: $\overrightarrow{OD}=-\mathbf a$.
(b) $\overrightarrow{BD}=\overrightarrow{BO}+\overrightarrow{OD}=-\mathbf b+(-\mathbf a)=-\mathbf a-\mathbf b$.
(c) $M$ is the midpoint of $BD$, so $\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OB}+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{BD}=\mathbf b+\tfrac12(-\mathbf a-\mathbf b)=\tfrac12\mathbf b-\tfrac12\mathbf a=\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$. From (a)(i), $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$, so $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}$: one vector is a scalar multiple of the other, so $OM$ is parallel to $AB$, and $OM:AB=1:2$.
mark_scheme: (a)(i) B1 for $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$; (ii) B1 for $-\mathbf a$
(b) M1 for a correct route, e.g. $\overrightarrow{BD}=\overrightarrow{BO}+\overrightarrow{OD}$; A1 for $-\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ (accept $-(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$)

(c) M1 for $\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OB}+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{BD}$ or $\tfrac12\left(\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OD}\right)$; A1 for $\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$ stated as $\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}$, a scalar multiple, hence parallel; A1 for $OM:AB=1:2$
common_errors: Reading $\overrightarrow{OD}$ as $\mathbf a$ because $OD$ and $OA$ have the same length, forgetting that the direction is reversed and so the sign must change.
In (c), giving $OM:AB=2:1$ by writing the ratio the wrong way round after correctly finding $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}$.

assets.caption: Regular hexagon $ABCDEF$ with centre $O$: $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, and $M$ the midpoint of the dashed segment $BD$.
assets.purpose: Give the printed hexagon the routes are read from, including the diagonal $OD$ that makes $\overrightarrow{OD}=-\mathbf a$ visible.

challenge_questions.statement: Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
challenge_questions.answer: The midpoint of diagonal $OB$ and the midpoint of diagonal $AC$ are the same point, $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let $OABC$ be a parallelogram, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$. Then $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf a+\mathbf c$, so the midpoint of $OB$ has position vector $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$. Also $\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf c-\mathbf a$, so the midpoint of $AC$ has position vector $\mathbf a+\tfrac12(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$. Both diagonals have the SAME midpoint, so the diagonals bisect each other.

challenge_questions.statement: In triangle $OAB$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, $N$ is the midpoint of $OB$ and $G$ is the point on $OM$ with $OG:GM=2:1$. Show that $A$, $G$, $N$ are collinear and find $AG:GN$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$, so $\overrightarrow{OG}=\tfrac23\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac13(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$. $\overrightarrow{AG}=\overrightarrow{OG}-\mathbf a=\tfrac13\mathbf b-\tfrac23\mathbf a$. $\overrightarrow{ON}=\tfrac12\mathbf b$, so $\overrightarrow{AN}=\tfrac12\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. Then $\overrightarrow{AG}=\tfrac23\left(\tfrac12\mathbf b-\mathbf a\right)=\tfrac23\overrightarrow{AN}$: parallel with common point $A$, hence $A$, $G$, $N$ are collinear, and $AG:GN=2:1$ (since $AG=\tfrac23AN$).

challenge_questions.statement: $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=k\mathbf a+3\mathbf b$. Find the value of $k$ for which $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{OC}-\overrightarrow{OB}=k\mathbf a+3\mathbf b-\mathbf b=k\mathbf a+2\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. For collinearity, $\overrightarrow{BC}=m\overrightarrow{AB}=-m\mathbf a+m\mathbf b$ for some scalar $m$: matching the $\mathbf b$-coefficients, $m=2$; matching the $\mathbf a$-coefficients, $k=-m=-2$.

challenge_questions.statement: In triangle $OAB$, $P$ is on $OA$ and $Q$ is on $OB$ with $OP:OA=OQ:OB=2:5$. Show that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$, and find the ratio of the area of triangle $OPQ$ to the area of the trapezium $PABQ$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac25\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\tfrac25\mathbf b$, so $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac25(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac25\overrightarrow{AB}$: parallel. Triangles $OPQ$ and $OAB$ are similar with scale factor $\tfrac25$, so their areas are in the ratio $\left(\tfrac25\right)^2:1^2=4:25$. The trapezium $PABQ$ has area $25-4=21$ parts (out of the same $25$), so $OPQ:PABQ=4:21$.

challenge_questions.statement: Three vertices of a parallelogram $ABCD$ (in that order) are $A(1,1)$, $B(5,2)$, $C(7,6)$. Find the coordinates of $D$ and the position vector of the point where the diagonals cross.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\end{pmatrix}$. In a parallelogram $\overrightarrow{DC}=\overrightarrow{AB}$, so $D=C-\overrightarrow{AB}=(7-4,\,6-1)=(3,5)$. The diagonals cross at the midpoint of $AC$ (or equally of $BD$): $\tfrac12\left(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}7\\6\end{pmatrix}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}4\\3.5\end{pmatrix}$. Check with $BD$: $\tfrac{5+3}2=4$, $\tfrac{2+5}2=3.5$.

mcq.stem: $A(2,5)$ and $B(7,1)$ have position vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. What is $\overrightarrow{AB}$?

options.why_wrong: Computes $\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ (start minus end) instead of $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$; this is actually $\overrightarrow{BA}$.
Adds $\mathbf a+\mathbf b$ instead of subtracting; addition is not the rule for a vector between two points.
Swaps the two components of the correct answer.

mcq.stem: $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$. What is $\overrightarrow{BO}$?

options.why_wrong: Forgets the minus sign that comes from travelling AGAINST the given arrow from $O$ to $B$.
There is no reason for the vector to double in length; reversing a vector's direction never changes its size, only its sign.
$\overrightarrow{BO}$ is only the zero vector if $B$ and $O$ are the same point; here $B$ is a distinct point, so the vector has the same length as $\mathbf b$, just reversed.

mcq.explanation: Travelling from $B$ back to $O$ is the exact reverse of travelling from $O$ to $B$, so $\overrightarrow{BO}=-\overrightarrow{OB}=-\mathbf b$.

mcq.stem: $P$ lies on $AB$ with $AP:PB=3:1$. What fraction of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is $\overrightarrow{AP}$?

options.why_wrong: Inverts the ratio, using the $PB$ part over the $AP$ part instead of the correct fraction.
Uses the ratio number on its own, forgetting that a fraction of the whole line requires dividing by the TOTAL number of parts.
Uses the $PB$ part ($1$) as the numerator over the correct total ($3+1=4$), instead of the $AP$ part ($3$) as the numerator.

mcq.explanation: $AP:PB=3:1$ splits $AB$ into $3+1=4$ equal parts, with $AP$ being $3$ of them: $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac{3}{3+1}\overrightarrow{AB}=\tfrac34\overrightarrow{AB}$.

mcq.stem: $\overrightarrow{PQ}=3\overrightarrow{AB}$, and $P$, $Q$, $A$, $B$ are four different points, with the segments $PQ$ and $AB$ not touching at all. What can you correctly conclude?

options.text: $P$, $Q$, $A$, $B$ all lie on one straight line (collinear).
options.why_wrong: Being a scalar multiple only proves the two segments are PARALLEL; without a shared point you cannot conclude they lie on one line — two parallel segments can be on entirely separate lines.
Nothing in the given information fixes any angles or equal side lengths; a scalar relationship between two vectors says nothing about the shape formed by the four points.

options.text: $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$, and three times as long.
$AB$ is three times as long as $PQ$.
options.why_wrong: Reverses the length ratio; since $\overrightarrow{PQ}=3\overrightarrow{AB}$, it is $PQ$ that is three times as long as $AB$, not the other way round.

mcq.explanation: A scalar multiple relationship between two vectors proves only that they are parallel (and gives their length ratio); collinearity cannot be concluded, because a collinearity proof needs the two vectors to share a point, and here they do not — the segments may lie on two separate parallel lines.

mcq.stem: Simplify $\mathbf a+\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$.

options.why_wrong: Expands the bracket but forgets to subtract $\tfrac12\mathbf a$ from the leading $\mathbf a$, leaving the expression unsimplified and with the wrong coefficient of $\mathbf a$.
Has the sign of the $\mathbf b$-term wrong; expanding the bracket correctly gives $+\tfrac12\mathbf b$, not $-\tfrac12\mathbf b$.
Adds $\tfrac12\mathbf a$ to $\mathbf a$ instead of subtracting it, getting the sign of the bracket's expansion wrong.

mcq.explanation: $\mathbf a+\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf b-\tfrac12\mathbf a=\tfrac12\mathbf a+\tfrac12\mathbf b$.

mcq.stem: $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, $P$ lies on $AB$ with $AP:PB=1:4$. What is $\overrightarrow{OP}$?

options.why_wrong: Swaps which point ($A$ or $B$) gets the larger coefficient; since $P$ is closer to $A$ (as $AP$ is the SMALLER part of the ratio), $\mathbf a$ should have the larger coefficient, not $\mathbf b$.
Uses the ratio numbers $1$ and $4$ directly as fractions out of $4$, instead of first adding them to get the correct total of $1+4=5$ parts.
The two coefficients do not add to $1$, which is impossible for any point actually lying on the line $AB$ — a quick check that rules this option out immediately.

mcq.explanation: $AP:PB=1:4$ means $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac{1}{1+4}\overrightarrow{AB}=\tfrac15(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$, so $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf a+\tfrac15(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\tfrac45\mathbf a+\tfrac15\mathbf b$.

flashcards.front: $\overrightarrow{AB}$ in terms of position vectors
flashcards.back: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$ — end minus start.

flashcards.front: What is a position vector?
flashcards.back: The vector $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ from a fixed origin $O$ to a point $A$.

flashcards.front: Triangle law
flashcards.back: $\overrightarrow{XY}+\overrightarrow{YZ}=\overrightarrow{XZ}$.

flashcards.front: True or false: travelling against a given arrow keeps the same sign.
flashcards.back: False. $\overrightarrow{YX}=-\overrightarrow{XY}$ — travelling against an arrow always introduces a minus sign.

flashcards.front: Position vector of the midpoint of $AB$
flashcards.back: $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$ — the AVERAGE of the two position vectors.

flashcards.front: If $AP:PB=m:n$, what is $\overrightarrow{AP}$?
flashcards.back: $\overrightarrow{AP}=\dfrac{m}{m+n}\overrightarrow{AB}$ — always add the parts of the ratio first.

flashcards.front: True or false: $AP:PB=2:1$ means $AP=\tfrac12AB$.
flashcards.back: False. $AP=\tfrac{2}{2+1}AB=\tfrac23AB$; always add the ratio's two parts to find the denominator.

flashcards.front: When are $PQ$ and $AB$ parallel?
flashcards.back: When $\overrightarrow{PQ}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$ for some scalar $k$; then $PQ=|k|\,AB$.

flashcards.front: True or false: showing $\overrightarrow{AB}\parallel\overrightarrow{PQ}$ always proves $A,B,P,Q$ are collinear.
flashcards.back: False. Parallel vectors with no shared point may lie on two DIFFERENT lines; collinearity also needs a common point.

flashcards.front: The two-part collinearity proof
flashcards.back: (1) Show $\overrightarrow{BC}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$ (parallel). (2) State that they share the point $B$, so $A,B,C$ are collinear.

flashcards.front: Parallel vs. collinear — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Parallel: one vector is a scalar multiple of the other (same or opposite direction). Collinear: parallel AND the vectors share a point, so all the points lie on ONE line.

flashcards.front: Similar triangles from a parallel line inside a triangle
flashcards.back: If $\overrightarrow{PQ}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$ (with $P$ on $OA$, $Q$ on $OB$), triangles $OPQ$ and $OAB$ are similar with scale factor $k$; their areas are in the ratio $k^2:1$.

flashcards.front: A route-method answer must always...
flashcards.back: ...be fully simplified into a single multiple of $\mathbf a$ plus a single multiple of $\mathbf b$, never left as an unsimplified chain of terms.

flashcards.front: Quick check for a ratio-point answer $\overrightarrow{OP}=p\,\mathbf a+q\,\mathbf b$
flashcards.back: $p+q$ must equal exactly $1$ for any point $P$ genuinely lying on the line $AB$ — a fast way to catch a ratio-to-fraction slip.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ (start minus end), instead of $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Reading the vector's name 'AB' left to right and listing $\mathbf a$ before $\mathbf b$ feels like it should give $\mathbf a$ first in the subtraction too, by analogy with reading order rather than with 'end minus start'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: Every route-method answer the learner produces comes out with the overall sign of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ reversed compared with the expected answer.
misconceptions.correct_model: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{AO}+\overrightarrow{OB}=-\mathbf a+\mathbf b=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$: the vector FROM $A$ TO $B$ is the position vector of the END ($B$) minus the position vector of the START ($A$), regardless of which letter is written first in the vector's own name.
misconceptions.remediation: Say the rule out loud as 'end minus start' every single time, rather than following the alphabetical order of the letters: for $\overrightarrow{BA}$ the end is $A$, so $\overrightarrow{BA}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Forgetting the minus sign when a route travels against a given arrow, for example writing $\overrightarrow{BO}=\mathbf b$ instead of $-\mathbf b$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The arrow for $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ is drawn once on the diagram, so it is easy to reuse the same label $\mathbf b$ whenever the route happens to retrace that arrow, without noticing that the route is travelling the opposite way along it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: In a multi-step route, exactly one term in the final simplified expression has the wrong sign compared with the expected answer, while the others are correct.
misconceptions.correct_model: Travelling AGAINST a given arrow always introduces a minus sign: if $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, then $\overrightarrow{BO}=-\mathbf b$. Before adding a vector into a route, check whether the route travels WITH or AGAINST its given arrow.
misconceptions.remediation: Mark every arrow on the diagram with its direction before starting, and as each leg of the route is used, say aloud whether it is 'with the arrow' (add it as given) or 'against the arrow' (add its negative).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Treating a ratio $AP:PB=m:n$ as the fraction $\tfrac{m}{n}$ of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, instead of $\tfrac{m}{m+n}$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A ratio such as $2:1$ visually resembles the fraction $\tfrac21$, so it is tempting to use the two ratio numbers directly as a fraction's numerator and denominator rather than first adding them to find how many equal parts the WHOLE line is split into.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's coefficients of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ in a ratio-point answer do not add to $1$ (they should always sum to exactly $1$ for any point lying on the line $AB$).
misconceptions.correct_model: $AP:PB=m:n$ splits $AB$ into $m+n$ equal parts, with $AP$ being $m$ of them: $\overrightarrow{AP}=\dfrac{m}{m+n}\overrightarrow{AB}$, and the resulting position vector $\overrightarrow{OP}=\left(1-\tfrac{m}{m+n}\right)\mathbf a+\tfrac{m}{m+n}\mathbf b$ always has coefficients summing to $1$.
misconceptions.remediation: After finding $\overrightarrow{OP}$, add its two coefficients as a check: if they do not sum to exactly $1$, an error has been made in converting the ratio to a fraction.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Believing that showing two vectors are parallel (one a scalar multiple of the other) is, by itself, enough to prove three points are collinear.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 'Parallel' and 'collinear' both involve one vector being a number times another, so the two ideas blur together; the extra requirement — that the two vectors compared must also SHARE a point — is an easy condition to forget once the scalar-multiple algebra is done.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's proof stops at 'therefore $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is parallel to $\overrightarrow{AB}$' when the question actually asked to prove that some SET OF NAMED POINTS lie on one line, without checking whether $PQ$ and $AB$ actually touch.
misconceptions.correct_model: A collinearity proof needs TWO things, not one: (1) the two vectors compared are parallel (one is a scalar multiple of the other), AND (2) they share a common point. Two parallel segments that do not touch (such as $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}$ in a similar-triangles diagram) are parallel but emphatically NOT part of the same straight line.
misconceptions.remediation: Before concluding a collinearity proof, name the shared point explicitly in the final sentence: 'therefore, since they are parallel and share the point $B$, $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Leaving a route-method answer as an unsimplified chain of terms, such as $-\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\tfrac12(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)$, instead of collecting the $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ terms into a single simplified expression.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Once every leg of the route has been added with the correct sign, the hard conceptual work feels finished, so the final algebraic simplification (collecting like terms) can be skipped under time pressure, especially when a fraction is involved.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's final answer to a route question still contains two or more separate terms in $\mathbf a$, or two or more separate terms in $\mathbf b$, rather than exactly one of each.
misconceptions.correct_model: A route-method answer is only finished once it is written as (a single number)$\times\mathbf a$ + (a single number)$\times\mathbf b$; collecting like terms is not optional polish, it is part of the method, and it is also what makes the parallel/collinear tests afterwards possible to read off at a glance.
misconceptions.remediation: After adding the legs of a route, go through the expression once more specifically to collect every $\mathbf a$-term together and every $\mathbf b$-term together, writing the simplified result on its own line.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ instead of $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$.
common_mistakes.why: Reading the name 'AB' left to right suggests listing $\mathbf a$ first in the subtraction too, rather than applying 'end minus start'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Say the rule out loud as 'end minus start' every time, not 'first letter minus second letter'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the minus sign when a route travels against a given arrow.
common_mistakes.why: The same arrow is drawn once on the diagram and labelled once, so reusing that label without a sign change is an easy slip when the route happens to retrace it backwards.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before adding a leg of a route, state out loud whether it travels WITH the given arrow (use it as given) or AGAINST it (use its negative).

common_mistakes.mistake: Concluding a collinearity proof after showing two vectors are parallel, without stating that they share a common point.
common_mistakes.why: The scalar-multiple algebra is the hard part, so once it's done the proof can feel finished, even though the 'shared point' condition has not yet been checked or stated.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: End every collinearity proof with an explicit sentence naming the shared point: 'parallel and share the point $B$, so $A,B,C$ are collinear.'

exam_notes: Vector geometry questions appear on Papers 2 and 4 (Extended) and are usually staged: 'Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$... Find $\overrightarrow{OM}$... Hence show that...'. Use each earlier part's answer in the next.

A correct scalar-multiple calculation without the closing sentence ('therefore parallel' / 'therefore collinear, sharing the point...') can lose the final accuracy mark, even when every line of algebra is right.

Give every final vector answer as a SIMPLIFIED single expression in $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ (one coefficient of $\mathbf a$, one of $\mathbf b$), written in bold, underlined, or with an arrow exactly as the question paper does.
A ratio-point answer $\overrightarrow{OP}=p\,\mathbf a+q\,\mathbf b$ should always have $p+q=1$; checking this is a fast way to catch a ratio-to-fraction conversion error before submitting an answer.

summary.big_idea: Every vector-geometry problem is solved by finding a route from known vectors, simplifying it into one multiple of $\mathbf a$ plus one multiple of $\mathbf b$, and then reading off parallel or collinear relationships directly from that simplified expression.
key_points: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$ (end minus start); $\overrightarrow{BA}=-\overrightarrow{AB}$; $\overrightarrow{XY}+\overrightarrow{YZ}=\overrightarrow{XZ}$.
Midpoint of $AB$: $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$. If $AP:PB=m:n$, then $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac{m}{m+n}\overrightarrow{AB}$ — always add the ratio's parts first.
Parallel: one vector is a scalar multiple of another. Collinear: parallel AND share a point — parallel alone is never enough.
If $\overrightarrow{PQ}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$, then $PQ=|k|AB$; a line cutting a triangle parallel to one side creates a similar triangle with area ratio $k^2:1$.
Always fully simplify a route-method answer into a single multiple of $\mathbf a$ plus a single multiple of $\mathbf b$ before using it further.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Find a route in known vectors, simplify fully, then check: is one vector a scalar multiple of another, and do they share a point? That is everything a parallel or collinear proof needs.

exercises.statement: The points $A(2,1)$, $B(3,4)$, $C(5,4)$ and $D(5,2)$ form a closed path $A\to B\to C\to D\to A$. (a) Describe the translation from A to B using a column vector. (b) Describe $\overrightarrow{BC}$, $\overrightarrow{CD}$ and $\overrightarrow{DA}$ as column vectors. (c) Given $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$, write down $-\mathbf{a}$ and $-\mathbf{b}$ as column vectors.
exercises.full_solution:
A column vector $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$ gives the movement in the $x$ direction (top) and the $y$ direction (bottom), so $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ = (coordinates of Q) $-$ (coordinates of P).

(a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}3-2\\4-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}$: 1 unit in the $x$ direction and 3 units in the $y$ direction.

(b) $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}5-3\\4-4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{CD}=\begin{pmatrix}5-5\\2-4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-2\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{DA}=\begin{pmatrix}2-5\\1-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. Check: the path is closed, so the four vectors add up to the zero vector: $1+2+0-3=0$ and $3+0-2-1=0$.

(c) A negative vector has the same length but the opposite direction, so both components change sign: $-\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-5\end{pmatrix}$ and $-\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked examples, Ch.31 'Translations' (column vectors AB, BC, CD, DA; vectors a, b; negative vectors -a, -b)

exercises.statement: Given $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$: (a) calculate $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$; (b) draw a diagram to represent $\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}$, where $\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{a}+(-\mathbf{b})$; (c) calculate the vector represented by $\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Add the components: $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}2+(-3)\\5+(-2)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$.

(b) Draw $\mathbf{a}$ (2 right, 5 up); from its end draw $-\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ (3 right, 2 up). The arrow from the start of $\mathbf{a}$ to the end of $-\mathbf{b}$ represents $\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}$.

(c) $\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}2-(-3)\\5-(-2)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\7\end{pmatrix}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked examples, 'Addition and subtraction of vectors' (a+b and a-b for a=(2,5), b=(-3,-2))

exercises.statement: (a) Given $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$, write $2\mathbf{a}$ as a column vector. (b) Given $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=-\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{c}=2\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{d}=\tfrac12\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{e}=-\tfrac32\mathbf{a}$, write $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{c}$, $\mathbf{d}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ as column vectors.
exercises.full_solution: Multiplying a column vector by a scalar $k$ multiplies both components by $k$. For $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-4\end{pmatrix}$: $\mathbf{b}=-\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\end{pmatrix}$; $\mathbf{c}=2\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-8\end{pmatrix}$; $\mathbf{d}=\tfrac12\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$; $\mathbf{e}=-\tfrac32\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\6\end{pmatrix}$. All four match the diagram's implied directions: $\mathbf{b}$ reverses $\mathbf{a}$; $\mathbf{c}$ doubles its length in the same direction; $\mathbf{d}$ halves it in the same direction; $\mathbf{e}$ is 1.5× longer and reversed.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked examples, 'Multiplying a vector by a scalar' (2a for a=(1,2); and b=-a, c=2a, d=(1/2)a, e=-(3/2)a for a=(2,-4))

exercises.statement: Given $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\8\end{pmatrix}$: (b.i) calculate $|\mathbf{a}|$; (b.ii) calculate $|\overrightarrow{BC}|$, using Pythagoras' theorem.
exercises.full_solution: The magnitude of $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$ is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{9+16}=\sqrt{25}=5$. $|\overrightarrow{BC}|=\sqrt{(-6)^2+8^2}=\sqrt{36+64}=\sqrt{100}=10$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked examples, 'The magnitude of a vector' (|a| for a=(3,4) and |BC| for BC=(-6,8))

exercises.statement: In a diagram, ABCD is a parallelogram-shaped quadrilateral (A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left) whose diagonals AC and BD intersect at E (E is the midpoint of both diagonals, since the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other). (a) Name a vector equal to $\overrightarrow{AD}$. (b) Write $\overrightarrow{BD}$ in terms of $\overrightarrow{BE}$. (c) Express $\overrightarrow{CD}$ in terms of $\overrightarrow{AB}$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Since ABCD is a parallelogram, side BC is parallel and equal in length to side AD, and both are traversed in the same rotational sense around the shape, so $\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AD}$. (b) E is the midpoint of diagonal BD (diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other), so $\overrightarrow{BE}=\overrightarrow{ED}$ and $\overrightarrow{BD}=\overrightarrow{BE}+\overrightarrow{ED}=2\overrightarrow{BE}$. (c) Side CD is parallel and equal to side AB but points in the opposite rotational direction around the parallelogram, so $\overrightarrow{CD}=\overrightarrow{BA}=-\overrightarrow{AB}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked examples, 'Vector geometry' (parallelogram ABCD with diagonals meeting at E: AD, BD in terms of BE, CD in terms of AB)

exercises.statement: A parallelogram (object) has vertices $(1,2)$, $(7,2)$, $(9,6)$ and $(3,6)$. Its reflected image has vertices $(1,-2)$, $(7,-2)$, $(9,-6)$ and $(3,-6)$. Find the equation of the mirror line.
exercises.full_solution: Each point of the image is the same perpendicular distance from a fixed line as the corresponding point of the object, on the opposite side. Comparing object vertex $(1,2)$ with image vertex $(1,-2)$: both have the same $x$-coordinate, and their $y$-coordinates are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign, so the midpoint of every object-image pair lies on $y=0$ and the segment joining them is vertical (perpendicular to $y=0$). Hence the mirror line is the $x$-axis, equation $y=0$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (a), Ch.32 'Reflection' - find the equation of the mirror line

exercises.statement: The diagram shows triangle $ABC$, with vertices $A(3,2)$, $B(5,2)$ and $C(4,4)$, together with its image $A'B'C'$ under an enlargement, with vertices $A'(5,3)$, $B'(9,3)$ and $C'(7,7)$. (The grid in the book carries no numbers, so the figure has been redrawn here on a numbered grid.) (a.i) Find the centre of enlargement. (a.ii) Calculate the scale factor of enlargement.
exercises.answer: (i) The centre of enlargement is $O(1,1)$: the lines $AA'$, $BB'$ and $CC'$ all meet there when they are extended backwards. (ii) The scale factor of enlargement is $2$.
exercises.full_solution:
To find the centre of enlargement, draw a straight line through each pair of corresponding points ($A$ and $A'$, $B$ and $B'$, $C$ and $C'$) and extend the lines backwards. An enlargement moves every point along a ray from one fixed centre, so all three lines must meet at that centre.

Line $AA'$ goes from $(3,2)$ to $(5,3)$, so its gradient is $\tfrac12$; going back 2 squares from $A$ gives $(1,1)$. Line $BB'$ goes from $(5,2)$ to $(9,3)$, gradient $\tfrac14$; going back 4 squares from $B$ gives $(1,1)$. Line $CC'$ goes from $(4,4)$ to $(7,7)$, gradient $1$; going back 3 squares from $C$ gives $(1,1)$. The three lines meet at $O(1,1)$.

For the scale factor, compare a pair of corresponding lengths: $AB=2$ and $A'B'=4$, so $k=\dfrac{4}{2}=2$. The distances from the centre agree: $OA=\sqrt{2^2+1^2}=\sqrt5$ and $OA'=\sqrt{4^2+2^2}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5$, so $OA'=2\times OA$. The scale factor of enlargement is $k=2$.
